apple contacts auth.description: Reports the current Contacts TCC state without prompting unless `--request` is passed. Add `--request` to ask macOS for Contacts permission explicitly without reading contact records or mutating the address book; if the executable lacks embedded Contacts usage metadata, the command refuses with an authorization error before making the request.

apple mail templates.description: Templates are `*.md` text files, one per template, in `~/.apple-cli/mail-templates/`. Set `APPLE_MAIL_TEMPLATES_DIR` to use another folder: it names the template folder itself, so `save` and `delete` act directly on the `*.md` files in it, and it should be a folder used only for templates. A leading `~` follows the same rules as the CLI's other path settings: `~`, `~/…` and `~yourname/…` mean your home folder, any other `~` form is refused as a `validation_error` (exit 64), and any other relative value is under the working directory.

apple messages recent.description: Returns recent Messages rows with the same JSON envelope as the rest of the CLI. Each message says which conversation it came from — `chat_identifier` and `chat_guid` (both `string|null`: null when the message maps to no chat row) and `is_group` (true when that chat's `style` is 43). A message joined to several chats reports the one with the lowest chat row id. `--direct-only` drops group-chat messages; the filter runs in SQL, before `--limit`, so a request for N messages still returns up to N rather than N-minus-the-groups. It excludes group chats specifically, not everything that is not a 1:1: a message belonging to no chat row at all is KEPT, because it is not in a group chat, and those are the ones with a null `chat_identifier`. A message that belongs to several chats is judged by the same lowest-row-id chat its `is_group` comes from, so a message in both a 1:1 and a group survives when the 1:1 chat has the lower row id and is excluded when the group does. The `direct_only` field echoes the flag back, and `direct_only_applied` says whether the filter actually ran — they differ only when the store cannot say which chat a message belongs to, in which case group messages are still present. Each message also includes `has_attachments` and an `attachments` array. Attachment paths are derived from chat.db metadata only: `filename` is the stored value, `path` is present only when an absolute standardized path can be derived, and `exists` is true or false only after a conservative local-root probe. When probing is skipped, `exists` is null.

examples.title: List recent messages with attachment metadata
Filter to an explicit synthetic handle
Read only 1:1 conversations, skipping group chats

apple messages recent.notes:
`messages recent` can include attachment-only messages that have no text body. Those rows use an empty `body` and carry the file details in `attachments`; a cache flag alone does not preserve a bodyless row when no joined attachment details exist. Attachment paths are not confined to the Messages attachments directory because sent items may point elsewhere on the local machine, but existence probing is limited to conservative local roots and uses symlink-aware traversal. Relative paths are omitted; automount and mounted-volume roots such as `/net`, `/home`, `/Network/Servers`, and `/Volumes` are reported without probing.

`group_name` and `chat_identifier` answer different questions and are not interchangeable: `group_name` is the chat's display name and is absent both for a 1:1 conversation and for a group that was never named, whereas `is_group` reports the chat's style directly, so an unnamed group still reads as a group. Any `chat.style` other than 43, including an absent or unrecognized one, is reported and filtered as non-group. A store old or pruned enough to lack `chat_message_join` reports null identifiers and `is_group: false` rather than failing the read, and `--direct-only` then excludes nothing, because nothing is known to be a group — that case sets `direct_only_applied: false` in the JSON and writes a warning to stderr, so a filter that could not be applied never passes silently on either channel.

apple messages search.description: Search returns scored message matches and carries the same chat identity and attachment shape as `messages recent`: `chat_identifier`, `chat_guid`, `is_group`, `has_attachments`, and per-file metadata in `attachments`. `--direct-only` drops group-chat hits, keeping messages that belong to no chat at all (they are not in a group chat, and carry a null `chat_identifier`). `search` has no `--limit`; the filter is applied before the internal cap on how many candidate messages are scored, so that budget goes to messages that can actually match. `direct_only` echoes the flag and `direct_only_applied` reports whether the filter actually ran. If the store cannot say which chat a message is in, the filter excludes nothing, `direct_only_applied` is false, and a warning goes to stderr. Any `chat.style` other than 43, including an absent or unrecognized one, is reported and filtered as non-group. This is additive under `schema_version` 1 because existing keys keep their names and types.

examples.title: Search recent messages and include attachment metadata
Search all retained message text exactly
Search 1:1 conversations only

apple messages search.notes: `messages search` first filters candidate rows by message text or attributed body, so an attachment-only row with no searchable body can appear in `messages recent` without appearing in search results. When a searched row does have joined attachments, the JSON includes the same metadata fields and conservative path-probe semantics as `messages recent`.

apple messages chats.description: Lists named chats with the id needed to send to them, plus how recently each was active and who is in it. `last_activity` is the ISO-8601 UTC date of the newest message in the chat; `last_activity_timestamp` is the RAW value chat.db stores for it, which is not a fixed unit — nanoseconds since the Apple epoch (2001-01-01 UTC) on modern rows but SECONDS on legacy ones, the same greater-than-10-digit heuristic a message's `timestamp` uses. Sorting on it is safe, between chats as well as within one, because a nanosecond value always exceeds a seconds value and the nanosecond rows are always the newer ones — a larger number is always a more recent message. Arithmetic on it is not: dividing by 1e9 gives a 1970 date on a chat whose newest message is old, and the difference between two of these values is meaningless when one is in each mode. Use `last_activity` for anything that treats the value as a time. Both are null for a chat with no messages. `participants` is the chat's handle ids (phone numbers or email addresses), possibly empty. They are raw, as chat.db stores them — not resolved to contact names the way a message's `sender` is — and they do not include you, since the store records only the other parties. The list is not deduplicated: one person can appear twice if the store holds a separate handle for them per service, so read it as a list rather than a set. `--name` keeps only chats whose display name contains the given text, case-insensitively, and is echoed back as `name_filter`; an EMPTY `--name` is treated as no filter at all and echoes null, so the field never claims a filter that did not narrow anything; `--limit` caps how many are returned and accepts 1-10000, rejecting anything outside that range with a validation error. Without either flag the listing is exactly what it always was: named chats only, in chat row order.

examples.title: List every named chat with its activity and members
Find a chat by part of its name
The first five named chats

apple messages chats.notes: Only NAMED chats are listed — a chat whose `display_name` is empty or absent (every 1:1 conversation, and any group nobody has named) does not appear, which is the behavior this command has always had. Ordering follows the chat table's own row order and `--name` and `--limit` do not change it: the filter is applied first, then the limit, so `--name X --limit 1` is the first chat matching X and not the first chat overall. A store that cannot be joined to its messages reports null activity rather than failing.

apple messages conversations.description: Discovers direct conversations, named groups and unnamed groups. Each row includes `chat_rowid`, `chat_guid`, `chat_identifier`, available display/service metadata, participants and last activity. `last_activity_normalized_seconds` and `last_activity_normalized_nanoseconds` provide the normalized Apple-epoch time as an exact pair, while `last_activity_timestamp` retains the raw database value. Use `chat_guid` or the local `chat_rowid` with `messages history` and `messages get`; display names and message text are not exact selectors. The existing `messages chats` command continues to list named chats only.

examples.title: Discover conversations of every kind
Continue the same discovery traversal

apple messages conversations.notes: Pages default to 100 rows and accept limits from 1 to 1000. Ordering is by normalized last activity, then chat ROWID; `--order desc` is the default and `--order asc` reverses it. Pass the returned `next_cursor` unchanged with the same order; null means there is no next page in this traversal. Cursors are limited to 4 KiB and are bound to the operation and ordering. Initial message and chat ROWID upper bounds exclude later inserts, including backdated messages, and conversation activity is computed only from messages within that bound. Each invocation reads a fresh snapshot, so edits, deletions and changed memberships can still affect later pages; this is not an immutable snapshot or event replay. The result limit does not bound database snapshot or discovery scan cost. Missing required schema or failed queries are errors rather than empty results. Reads do not drive Messages UI or mark conversations read.

apple messages history.description: Reads one exact conversation with bounded results. Supply exactly one of `--chat-guid` or `--chat-rowid`. GUIDs are opaque database identifiers; ROWIDs are positive identifiers local to this Messages database. Ambiguous GUIDs are refused. A message linked to several chats retains the selected conversation's identity, rather than silently switching to its first chat.

examples.title: Read an explicitly selected local conversation
Continue that conversation's history

apple messages history.notes:
Pages default to 100 rows, with a maximum of 1000. Messages sort by normalized Apple timestamp and message ROWID, newest first unless `--order asc` is supplied. Undated rows remain discoverable. `timestamp` retains the raw Apple value; `normalized_seconds` and `normalized_nanoseconds` form an exact pair since the Apple epoch (2001-01-01 UTC), with a nonnegative nanosecond remainder. Both normalized fields are null for undated rows. Reuse `next_cursor` unchanged with the same resolved conversation and order; null marks the end. Cursors are limited to 4 KiB. A first-page message ROWID upper bound excludes later inserts even when their dates are older. Each page reads a fresh snapshot: edits, deletions and membership changes remain visible, so this is not snapshot isolation across invocations or a resume/replay event stream. Output limits do not bound snapshot cost.

Each message exposes `message_guid` and the selected chat identity alongside its local ROWID and message/attachment fields. Bodyless and undecodable records are retained; `body_availability` distinguishes them from available text. Exact reads also decode a constrained, data-only subset of `attributedBody` native-part metadata. `native_parts_available` is true when the archive is decoded; `native_parts` is an array of `{index, utf16_ranges, attachment_guid}` records. Each index is scoped to the enclosing message GUID; neither attachment order nor a text offset is used as native identity. The array is empty with `native_parts_reason: "empty-known"` when a supported archive has no native-part keys. `utf16_ranges` are offsets into the archived attributed-string text, not necessarily the emitted `body` value, because the database `text` column still has body precedence. Missing archives report `native_parts_available: false`, `native_parts: null`, `native_parts_reason: "absent-blob"`; malformed, keyed, or richer unsupported archives also report false/null with a bounded reason rather than partial metadata. Exact reads also include an always-present `thread_originator` object. When both native originator columns exist and both values are null or empty, it reports `available: true` and `reason: "no-linkage"`; when either column is absent, it reports `available: false`, `reason: "missing-schema"` and explicit null values. Valid linkage preserves the raw GUID and raw part marker and parses only a canonical ASCII nonnegative integer prefix before the first colon. Partial metadata, wrong SQLite storage types, noncanonical prefixes, overflows and the UInt64.max marker are unavailable rather than guessed, and the field does not claim an immediate parent/root or authorize mutation. Missing required schema, failed queries and missing conversation identities fail clearly. Reading history does not mark the conversation read. Exact reads include an always-present `native_status` object with `error`, `is_delivered`, `is_read`, `date_delivered` and `date_read`. Each field has `status` and nullable integer `raw`; error adds nullable `is_error`, flags add nullable `value`, and timestamps add nullable `normalized_seconds`, `normalized_nanoseconds`, `date` (UTC) and `date_local`. All listed keys are explicitly encoded, including nulls. Missing columns report `missing-schema`, SQL NULL reports `null`, and noninteger storage reports `wrong-type` without coercing its bytes. Error integers are preserved and `is_error` means only raw != 0; no error-name dictionary is inferred. Flags accept only integer 0/1; other integers retain raw with `invalid-boolean` and null value. Timestamp 0 is `zero-sentinel`; negatives report `negative`; parsed fields are null in both cases. Positive values use the existing compatibility heuristic: at most 9,999,999,999 means seconds since 2001-01-01 UTC, larger values mean nanoseconds since that Apple epoch. Normalized values are whole seconds plus a nonnegative subsecond remainder, not total nanoseconds. Strings use whole-second Gregorian/POSIX formatting; raw and remainder preserve precision. Unrepresentable formatting reports `invalid-timestamp` with raw retained and parsed fields null. Valid values report `available`. Flags and dates are independent observations and never inferred from one another. Their interpretation depends on message direction and native Messages behavior; these row-level fields are not per-recipient group receipts, a cross-device synchronization guarantee, or proof for sending or other mutations.

apple messages get.description: Fetches one message using exactly one conversation selector (`--chat-guid` or `--chat-rowid`) and exactly one message selector (`--message-guid` or `--message-rowid`). Both identities and their membership are checked in the read-only database snapshot. Duplicate GUIDs, missing rows and a message outside the selected conversation are refused. Identical text in another conversation does not affect selection.

examples.title: Fetch one message in its selected conversation

apple messages get.notes: GUIDs are opaque, persistent identifiers when available; positive ROWIDs are local to this database. The result retains caller-selected chat membership even when the message also belongs to another conversation. Message, attachment, native-part and `thread_originator` fields use the same shape as `messages history`, including explicit body availability, explicit native-part null-versus-array states and explicit nullable thread-originator keys. This command reads database state only; it does not select a Messages window, mark a chat read or mutate a message. The always-present `native_status` object has the same per-field availability, explicit nulls, raw integer values and Apple-epoch timestamp semantics documented under `messages history`; it is native row metadata, not per-recipient delivery/read guarantees or mutation authority.

apple messages automation.description: Reads or explicitly recovers the shared Messages UI automation journal used by experimental reaction writes.

examples.title: Read the shared automation state
Preview explicit recovery

apple messages automation.notes: Reaction writes record pending state before handing work to the UI worker. A timeout, cancellation, failed verification or crash after possible handoff leaves that state unresolved and blocks later Messages UI writes. Status is read-only. Recovery is explicit and requires acknowledgement of possible late effects; it is not a proof that Messages cancelled or quiesced the original request.

apple messages automation status.description: Reads the shared Messages automation journal state without driving Messages or clearing anything. It reports the pending operation, if any, plus bounded receipts for resolved or recovered operations.

examples.title: Check for a pending Messages automation operation

apple messages automation status.notes: A pending record gates new Messages UI writes until the original operation reaches observed state or is explicitly recovered. The status output includes `pending` as null or `{operation_id, operation_type, phase}` and `receipts` as `{operation_id, disposition}` records. It does not expose message bodies, recipient addresses or other target values. Reads use the same locked private state root as reaction writes.

apple messages automation recover.description: Explicitly clears a pending Messages automation operation after the operator acknowledges possible late effects. It is for uncertain post-handoff states such as timeout, cancellation, failed verification or crash after a request may have reached Messages.

examples.title: Preview recovery for one pending operation
Recover after acknowledging possible late effects

apple messages automation recover.notes: Recovery requires `--acknowledge-possible-late-effects`; without it the command refuses. Dry run verifies that the named operation exists and is in an uncertain-after-handoff phase but does not clear it. Execution records a recovered receipt and removes the pending gate. Recovery does not prove cancellation, quiescence, sync completion or correctness of the original UI action; it only acknowledges the risk so later writes can proceed. Use `messages automation status` first and recover only the exact operation id it reports.

apple messages reaction.description: Groups exact Messages reaction inspection and experimental standard and custom-emoji writes. Reads are database-only; writes execute by default unless `--dry-run` or `APPLE_DRY_RUN=1` is active and always report `experimental: true`.

examples.title: Inspect reactions for one message
Preview setting a standard reaction

apple messages reaction.notes: Reaction writes use exact conversation, message and native-part identity. Agent-run live writes must use the sandbox. The sandbox requires the target message text to start with `apple-cli-test`, requires exactly one selected participant, and confines that participant to the allowed test recipients; sandbox reaction writes refuse group conversations. Production writes may target exact group chat GUIDs or ROWIDs. Standard reactions are `heart`, `like`, `dislike`, `laugh`, `emphasize` and `question`. Custom emoji set/replace is experimental: it verifies an already-selected exact Tapback button as unchanged, and uses the uniquely owned native chooser when that button is unselected or absent. Unknown selected state is refused. Live reliability remains unverified. Explicit custom removal with `--emoji` uses an exact, byte-matched native picker button; a bounded settling interval precedes its single press and exact-state revalidation. Missing buttons never prove that a reaction is absent. Successful writes require native picker selected-state verification plus fresh database target identity and eligibility; raw database authorship is returned as recorded and is not used alone to prove the current user’s reaction.

apple messages reply.description: Groups experimental exact threaded reply sends for Messages. The current subcommand sends either bounded text or one single-file attachment reply to an exact message in a direct conversation.

examples.title: Preview an exact text reply
Preview an exact attachment reply

apple messages reply.notes: Reply sends are experimental UI handoffs. Dry run resolves the exact selected target, its supported thread relationship, and sandbox policy without driving Messages UI or creating journal state; attachment dry runs also resolve the shared attachment source and preview the selected file path, basename and byte count without creating a draft copy. Execution requires `--experimental-ui-handoff`, the shared Messages automation journal, Accessibility trust and a direct one-recipient conversation. Group replies are not enabled in this unit. Agent-run live writes must use the sandbox and target only operator-approved test recipients.

apple messages reply send.description: Sends a bounded text reply or one single-file attachment reply to one exact message in a direct Messages conversation. Select the conversation with exactly one of `--chat-rowid` or `--chat-guid`; select the message with exactly one of `--message-rowid` or `--message-guid`; pass `--part-index` for the decoded native part and exactly one of `--body` or `--file` for reply content.

examples.title: Preview a sandboxed exact text reply
Preview a sandboxed exact attachment reply
Execute a text reply with explicit UI handoff opt-in
examples.command: APPLE_TEST_MODE=1 apple messages reply send --chat-rowid 42 --message-rowid 123 --part-index 2 --body 'apple-cli-test reply' --experimental-ui-handoff

examples.title: Execute an attachment reply with explicit UI handoff opt-in

apple messages reply send.notes: Pass exactly one of `--body` or `--file`. Text replies must be nonempty and at most 2048 UTF-8 bytes; `--body` is used instead of `--text` because `--text` is the global output-format flag. Attachment replies accept one local regular file through the shared attachment source policy, capped at 25 MiB. The private draft copy retains the resolved source filename and extension. Its filename must be at most 255 UTF-8 bytes and cannot contain a slash, NUL, or ASCII control character. Verification requires unchanged file content: if Messages transforms or reencodes the attachment, a size or hash mismatch leaves the operation uncertain even if the file was sent. Do not resend to resolve that uncertainty. Execution copies that file into an operation-owned private draft location before the UI handoff, pastes exactly once, accepts only the observed native attachment marker shape as pre-send UI readiness, posts one Return key pair, and then requires strict database proof for one fresh outgoing reply row in the selected chat with integer `is_sent = 1` and `error = 0`, plus one attachment join whose safe Messages attachment file matches the copied content hash and size. Pending send status is polled within the operation deadline; unavailable, malformed or failed status cannot verify success. This is local observed state, not a recipient-delivery or cross-device synchronization guarantee. Draft UI metadata is not treated as file identity proof. Successful text results report `verification_source: ui_clean_state_and_database_correspondence`; successful attachment results report `verification_source: ui_clean_state_database_correspondence_and_attachment_content` and an `attachment` object with `attachment_rowid`, `attachment_guid`, `attachment_filename`, `attachment_sha256`, `attachment_size`, and `copy_cleanup`. The private copy is reclaimed only after the journal durably records observed success. `copy_cleanup: complete` means reclamation finished; `incomplete` means some private staging content may remain, with `copy_directory` identifying its directory for inspection. Incomplete copy cleanup does not reverse a verified send and must not prompt a resend. A process crash between journal resolution and reclamation can also leave staging content behind. Both modes report `sent_message_rowid`, `sent_message_guid`, `parent_message_guid`, `parent_native_part`, and the exact target. Dry run performs no UI work, creates no journal entry, and for attachments creates no draft copy. If Messages already restored the clean main composer after send, no cancel is sent; if an owned reply composer remains empty, exactly one `AXCancel` closes it. The command preserves nonempty drafts on failure because the native marker cannot prove attachment ownership. After the first send dispatch, it never retries Return. Database thread-originator metadata alone never authorizes a write; the parent accepts the worker ACK only after strict same-chat new-row proof. If verification or UI/clipboard cleanup fails after handoff, the command reports uncertainty and acknowledges the send may have occurred. Nested targets require one unambiguous, single-part selected message linked to one unique single-part root in the same direct conversation. Multi-hop chains and group replies remain unsupported. The selected message and resolved root are bound independently through preflight and final verification. The target includes selected `is_from_me` and a `thread_root` object; `root_is_from_me` continues to describe the root. Messages may persist the thread root instead of the selected reply as the new row's originator. Such a result requires the verified UI ACK, an unchanged bound relationship, and exactly one fresh owned outgoing row in the bounded scan, including unrelated outgoing text or attachments when checking ambiguity. Both strict and thread-root judges use that same scan. The result adds `observed_thread_originator`, `persisted_parent_matches_requested`, and `reply_relationship` (`requested-target` or `thread-root`). Existing `parent_message_guid` and `parent_native_part` always describe the observed native pair. A thread-root result establishes thread correspondence, not a database-proven immediate parent. Existing `verification_source` values remain unchanged; `verification` explicitly describes thread-root correspondence when applicable. Dry-run previews contain no observed relationship result. A verification-stage window or relationship drift may include a value-free reason suffix; it remains a refusal and never causes a retry.

apple messages reaction inspect.description: Inspects the current reaction state for one exact Messages target. Supply exactly one conversation selector (`--chat-guid` or `--chat-rowid`) and exactly one message selector (`--message-guid` or `--message-rowid`). The command reads chat.db only; it does not open Messages, mark a conversation read or mutate a reaction.

examples.title: Inspect reactions on one local message
Inspect one native message part with a smaller row cap

apple messages reaction inspect.notes: `--part-index` selects one native Messages part index decoded from `attributedBody`. Without it, a message with exactly one decoded native part uses that part; a message with several decoded parts reports `multiple-native-parts-require-explicit-part`, and a message whose native parts are unavailable reports why the part could not be proven. `--row-limit` defaults to 512 and accepts 1 through 10000. If more matching reaction rows exist than the cap, the JSON reports `rows_capped: true`, includes `reaction-row-limit-exceeded` in `unknown_reasons`, and treats the fold as unknown rather than pretending the partial scan is authoritative. Author fields and `current_outgoing` describe raw database attribution. In a self-chat, Messages may replace an outgoing reaction event with an incoming echo even while the local picker still shows the reaction selected. Inspection does not open the picker or infer local ownership from an incoming handle; reaction writes report their separate native UI verification source.

apple messages reaction set.description: Sets or replaces the outgoing reaction on one exact Messages target. Supply exactly one conversation selector (`--chat-guid` or `--chat-rowid`) and one message selector (`--message-guid` or `--message-rowid`); `--part-index` selects a decoded native part. Use exactly one of `--reaction` for a standard reaction or `--emoji` for a custom reaction. Standard and custom set/replace are experimental. Custom reactions verify an already-selected exact Tapback button as unchanged; an unselected or absent button uses a uniquely owned emoji chooser. Unknown selected state, unsupported controls and ambiguous controls are refused.

examples.title: Preview setting a heart reaction
Execute a standard reaction with explicit modal handoff opt-in
examples.command: APPLE_TEST_MODE=1 apple messages reaction set --chat-rowid 42 --message-rowid 123 --reaction heart --experimental-ui-handoff

apple messages reaction set.notes: Dry run resolves the exact target and sandbox policy without driving UI or creating journal state. Execution checks the requested native picker button before deciding whether to press; an already-selected reaction performs no reaction click. The `--experimental-ui-handoff` flag only opts into the native picker transition that can hide the transcript; it does not choose the post-press verification branch. In either strict or experimental mode, the `.present` branch verifies the requested selected state on the same retained picker and button, then cancels that owned picker and verifies dismissal before ACK. If the picker disappears before state proof, the same `.absent` branch restores the exact original process, root, window, transcript and message identity route, confirms the picker is absent immediately before opening the canonical menu from that retained message, then verifies the requested selected state and owned cleanup. If the disappearance comes from a hidden-transcript transition, `--experimental-ui-handoff` must have been supplied. The fallback does not require the message to remain selected and does not deep-link or navigate to another message. Changed identities, unavailable controls, ambiguous ownership, a failed state check or cleanup failure leave the result uncertain. No branch repeats the reaction click. The parent accepts ACK only when bound to the pending operation and records observed state only after fresh database target identity and eligibility verification. Results report `reaction_changed` and `verification_source: ui_selected_state_and_database_identity`. `executed` means UI automation ran; it does not imply a reaction changed. Raw database author fields remain unchanged and may differ from local picker state in self-chats. The experimental handoff opt-in cannot prove original-message continuity during the modal transition, cancellation quiescence inside Messages or durable sync completion. Leave Messages untouched during execution. Preview and result identify `targeting_mode`; opt-in output explains the limitation. For a custom reaction whose exact Tapback button is unselected or absent, the chooser uses a search term and exact result index obtained through an optional macOS CharacterPicker private framework. Unavailable lookup, incomplete results, duplicate exact matches or changed ownership cause refusal. Launcher recognition currently requires the native English Accessibility description; other UI languages are not validated and may refuse. The requested emoji is compared byte-for-byte, including variation selectors, skin tones and ZWJ sequences; search terms never authorize a different emoji. The chooser uses bounded Down/Right/Return navigation in the native six-column result grid, posting keys only to Messages and checking process, chooser ownership and query between keys. Results requiring a separate skin-tone picker are refused; no default-tone substitution occurs. Native result order and layout are private macOS behavior, and other layouts are not validated. On a failure before keyboard navigation, it restores its search only while the retained field still contains the value it wrote. Return is attempted once, without an AXPress fallback, and the resulting reaction must be verified on the original message. Support for every emoji variant and general live reliability are not established.

apple messages reaction remove.description: Removes an outgoing reaction from one exact Messages target. Select the target with the same exact chat/message/native-part selectors as `reaction set`. Pass `--reaction` for a standard reaction or `--emoji` for explicit custom-emoji removal. Omit both only when database evidence resolves exactly one outgoing standard reaction. Explicit custom removal is experimental and requires an exact native picker button. A bounded settling interval precedes the single press, with exact-state revalidation after the wait. Implicit custom removal remains refused outside dry run.

examples.title: Preview removing a like reaction
Execute an explicit removal with handoff opt-in
examples.command: APPLE_TEST_MODE=1 apple messages reaction remove --chat-rowid 42 --message-rowid 123 --reaction like --experimental-ui-handoff

apple messages reaction remove.notes: The same exact-target, dry-run, sandbox, pending-operation and UI verification rules as `reaction set` apply. An explicit requested reaction is removed only if its native button is selected; an unselected button is a verified no-change result with `reaction_changed: false`. Database outgoing absence alone never proves local UI absence. When the database cannot resolve one reaction for implicit removal, specify `--reaction` or `--emoji` explicitly; the command refuses instead of guessing or reporting a false no-op. The `--experimental-ui-handoff` flag only opts into transcript-hidden picker transitions; retained-picker `.present` proof and restored-route `.absent` proof are post-press verification branches available under the same identity rules described for `reaction set`. Results report `reaction_changed` and `verification_source: ui_selected_state_and_database_identity` while retaining raw database authorship. The experimental handoff opt-in cannot prove original-message continuity during the modal transition, cancellation quiescence inside Messages or durable sync completion. Leave Messages untouched during execution. Post-verification cannot undo a reaction redirected by desktop interference. Custom emoji identifiers are matched byte-for-byte, including variation selectors, skin tones and ZWJ sequences; the command never substitutes a base emoji. A repeated custom removal is a verified no-op only when the exact button is still exposed and unselected. A missing button is not evidence of absence. If the button disappears after a press, verification fails and the operation remains pending instead of claiming success. General custom-removal idempotency and live reliability are not established.

apple messages send.description: Sends when invoked; `--dry-run` previews. `--service` picks the route for a one-to-one send: `auto` (the default) tries iMessage and falls back to SMS for a phone-shaped recipient, `imessage` uses iMessage only and fails rather than falling back, and `sms` uses the enabled SMS account only. `--file` attaches a file and may be repeated; the message body goes out first, then each file in the order given, all in one Messages automation run. Either a message or a file is required — a send with neither is a `validation_error`, reported after the recipient has been resolved, so an unknown recipient or a sandbox refusal comes first.

examples.title: Preview a send without sending it

apple messages send.notes:
`--service` applies to one-to-one sends only. It is accepted with `--group` and has no effect there: a chat id already names the chat's own service, and Messages offers no choice. The flag is still reported back as `service_requested` so a caller can see it was ignored rather than silently honoured. `--service sms` to a recipient with no digits in it is refused up front as a `validation_error` (exit 64), because SMS cannot reach one. The test is literally "does this contain a digit", the same one the `auto` fallback uses, so an address like `jane.doe1@example.com` passes it and fails later inside Messages instead; `auto` and `imessage` reach email addresses normally.

`--file` works with `--group` too, and each file then goes to the whole chat rather than to one person. That path is pinned at the command layer and its AppleScript is compile-checked, but it has never been run against a live group, so treat the delivery behaviour as designed and unverified. The sandbox (`--test-mode` / `APPLE_TEST_MODE`) refuses group sends outright and still confines one-to-one recipients to `APPLE_TEST_RECIPIENTS`; neither flag changes that.

The JSON carries `service_requested` (`auto`/`imessage`/`sms`) and `files` (the attachment paths, `[]` when there are none) on both the dry-run and the execute envelope; the execute envelope adds `files_sent`, which is absent from a dry run because nothing was sent. On a dry run, `service_plan` reads `iMessage→SMS auto`, `iMessage only`, `SMS only`, or `group chat`. A file-only send reports no `message` key.

Every `--file` path goes through the same guard `mail send --attach` uses, and the whole batch is checked before anything is dispatched. A path is resolved to an absolute, SYMLINK-RESOLVED location — a link is sent, and reported in `files`, as the file it points at — and it must be an existing regular file (`not_found`, exit 65, otherwise; that is also what an `.app` bundle gets, since a bundle is a directory). Refused outright: anything inside a credential or config directory (`~/.ssh`, `~/.gnupg`, `~/.config`, `~/.aws`, `~/.claude`, `~/Library/Keychains`, `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, `~/Library/LaunchDaemons`), checked after symlinks are resolved so a link into one cannot slip past; executable and script file types (`.sh`, `.command`, `.exe`, `.app` as a single file, and the rest of the same list Mail blocks); anything over 25 MB; any path containing a control character; and a path spelled as another user's home (`~user/…`, any account but your own — a `validation_error`, exit 64, decided before the path is expanded; your own account's `~name/…` means the same as `~/…`). The credential and control-character refusals are `safety_violation` (exit 77), the type and size refusals `validation_error` (exit 64). The argument is never trimmed, so a filename with a leading or trailing space names that file and not its neighbour. `--dry-run` refuses exactly what an execute would.

The check is path-based, and it is worth knowing what that excludes: a hard link to a credential file is a second name for the same bytes and is not detected (no more than `cp` would be), and the file is read by Messages after the check rather than during it, so a path can be swapped in between. Both are inherited from the Mail attachment guard.

A send is not atomic: the body and each attachment are separate transfers, so a failure partway through leaves the earlier ones delivered. When an attachment was in flight, that is an `upstream_error` naming which attachment failed, how many had already gone out, and the paths already delivered (in `error.applied`). When none was — the body went out and then, say, the SMS account lookup failed — the error is the generic one, with no attachment named and no `applied` list. Either way, if the message body itself had already gone out, the error says so explicitly and tells you to omit `--message` from the retry. If Messages returns a result this version cannot read, the error says that what was delivered is unknown — the message and any attachments may have gone in full — and asks you to check the conversation before retrying, because the retry advice above cannot be derived from counters that were never observed; the error envelope's `remediation` field then begins `delivery unknown:` so a script can detect the state without parsing the message.

apple notes search.description: Searches note titles, or note bodies instead of titles with `--content`, across the account or within one folder with `--folder`. `--folder` must name at least one path component: `""` and separators-only values such as `"///"` are refused as a `validation_error` (exit 64) rather than silently widening the search to the whole account. Omit `--folder` to search every folder.

apple notes recent.description: Returns the notes in scope ordered by modification date, newest first, cut to `--limit` (default 10). Each hit is the same `NoteSummary` shape `apple notes search` emits — `id`, `title`, `content` (always `""`), `tags` (always `[]`), `folder`, `account`, `created`, `modified` — so anything that already consumes a search hit consumes a recent hit unchanged. The envelope carries `notes`, `count`, `applied_limit`, `limit_reached`, and `sync_warning` when an iCloud sync is in progress. With no `--account` the scope is the **default account only** (iCloud), not every account; `--account` selects a different one. `--folder` narrows further and accepts a nested path (`Parent/Child`, with `\/` escaping a literal slash in a folder name).

apple notes recent.notes:
**Notes in Recently Deleted are enumerated.** Deleting a note updates its modification date, so a note you just deleted can be the most recently modified note in the account and lead this list. A hit's `folder` identifies it, and passing `--folder` scopes past the trash. There is no exclusion flag yet: the trash folder's AppleScript name is localized and Notes exposes no "deleted" property, so filtering it needs a design rather than a name match.

`limit_reached` is true when more notes were in scope than `--limit` asked for. Read that field, not `count`: a note can be ranked and then fail to read back — deleted between the two reads, untitled, or unreadable — and nothing backfills from the next candidate, so `count` can be below `applied_limit` while the scope still holds more. (`apple notes search` carries the same key with a weaker meaning: it stops looking at the limit, so it reports that more results MAY exist. Here the whole scope was ranked before the cut, so it reports that more DO.)

A note whose modification date Notes.app cannot report is ranked last rather than treated as just-modified. **Its `modified` value is a placeholder — the time it was read, not a fact about the note** — so do not re-sort the array by `modified` and do not display that date; the order this command returns is the reliable signal. Every other hit's `modified` is the value the ranking used, so the array order and the dates in it always agree. Notes with the same modification date (second granularity makes ties ordinary) are ordered by `id`, so repeated runs return the same list.

The command runs as two reads: one bulk read of every note's id and modification date in scope — two property reads for the scope however large, rather than a round trip per note — then the full per-note read for the few that survive the cut. So the per-note reads track `--limit`, while the id-and-date enumeration still touches the whole scope at that fixed cost. Measured on a few-hundred-note library: 1.1s at `--limit 5`, 1.7s at the default 10, 6.4s at `--limit 50`.

**There is no fixed time limit on this command.** The 45-second AppleScript timeout bounds one Apple event's reply — not a script, not the command, and not the in-process loop that renders the bulk read, which is bounded by nothing. The number of events grows with the scope and with `--limit`, and each of the two scripts is retried once if an event times out. Any single event exceeding 45 seconds surfaces as `upstream_error`, exit 69, "Notes.app timed out…". The bulk read is retried once for one further reason: if its id and date lists come back at different lengths the note set changed mid-read, which a second attempt normally resolves; a mismatch that survives both attempts is reported as `upstream_error`, exit 69, with its own message rather than a generic one.

A hit's `folder` is the name of the folder holding the note; when Notes.app cannot report a note's container the field carries the literal `Notes`, which is the fallback the underlying script substitutes rather than a folder of that name — the key is never absent and never empty.

`--limit` must be greater than 0, and `--folder` must name at least one path component (both `""` and `"///"` are refused); either failure is a `validation_error`, exit 64, raised before Notes.app is contacted. `--text` renders one line per note as `modified  title  (folder)` with an ISO-8601 timestamp, showing that same `folder` value; a note whose modification date could not be read (ranked last, see above) shows `modified: unknown` in place of the timestamp.
